utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I remind you that the affirmation you made still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic. Still -- I'm living in over-eager hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's still me but not for much longer, Your Honour, I assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Wonderful, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Yesterday when he left off we were speaking about the Racak incident and the different meetings you had with the MUP and VJ officials in relation to this incident. Before moving on to a different topic, I would just like to look at one more of the attachments to your statement. This is attachment number 7 which relates to this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, that this attachment is now Exhibit P863, and I need page 1 in both the English and B/C/S of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have the document before you, General?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a record of discussions of a meeting at the VJ brigade command at Urosevac dated 4th February, 1999, and we see from this record that in attendance in addition to yourself are MR. -- Colonel Kotur; Colonel Krsman Jelic, the commander of the 243rd Brigade; and Pera Petrovic of whom we spoke about yesterday; and other persons who are listed there. Do you recall attending this meeting, General?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you speak about this briefly in your statement - this is at paragraph 30 to 32. So I just want to look at some passages here. On the first page towards the bottom, you are recorded as addressing Colonel Jelic and asking him: "Did you order the forces to do this, if not, who was the commander on the ground?" And if you turn to the next page, we have Colonel Jelic who responses - that's on page 2 in the middle of the first paragraph. We see that he is explaining -- giving you an explanation of what happened and he says: "Unit as Stimlje was training and was fired upon," in some sentences down it says, "fired was made on targets between Belince and Racak, provocations came from there." Now, based on the understandings you had at the time of the October agreements were VJ units allowed to conduct training activities outside of barracks and in the proximity of inhabited areas at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see here that further down you are asking Colonel Jelic about this operation and he says: "Our operation happened at the same time of the MUP operation," and you ask him on 15 January between 8 and 9.00 a.m. and he says, "Yes." Do you recall when you left this meeting with Colonel Jelic if you were convinced by the explanation he gave you at the meeting that the unit was simply conducting a training exercise and that this training exercise happened at the same time as the MUP operation was taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not convinced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been because of the -- the emotional stress that I was under having been, you know, having seen the aftermath of the -- of the activity. And it also just did not seem plausible to me that -- that, you know, a coordinated MUP action with VJ, you know, having by happenstance been in that area would make sense. There's no doubt if, first of all, the VJ had been doing some training, that they would have known that the MUP were going to be in the village. And there's no way that, you know, there's no way they would have done this independently without coordinating together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now move away from the Racak incident to a different issue, and I want to refer you to paragraph 9 of your statement, where you refer to a meeting you had with Mr. Sainovic, and this is a meeting that took place on one of the occasions when you officially replaced General DZ or Drewienkiewicz, also known as DZ. Do you recall attending this meeting? The one that's referred to at paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this meeting took place, and what was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember which -- in which of the periods that I replaced DZ which are laid out in my statement here, but I don't remember exactly on which one of those periods that I met with him. The purpose of the meeting was for -- I think it was a regular meeting between Ambassador Keller and Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on the information you had at the time, what did you understand to be Mr. Sainovic's role in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I remember, you know, I don't know if I knew that exactly at the time, but I obviously since know that he was responsible for Kosovo. I understand since then that he was the minister responsible of Kosovo delegated by the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you understand him at the time to have any authority over either VJ or MUP units that were deployed on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly something that I remember absolutely is that I had no doubt in my mind at the time, and since either, that he had -- he had full authority to control and command and give direction to the units that were deployed within the theatre of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what made you arrive to that conclusion, that he had full authority, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a combination of the manner in which he behaved, the manner in which he carried himself, the manner in which he responded to the questions by Ambassador Keller. And I don't remember exactly the different issues that were being discussed, but it seemed to me that there were no -- there was no question that he was in charge of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now move to a different issue, and this is one of the last topics I want to discuss with you. This concerns the paragraph 56 of your statement and refers to the period when you had already left Kosovo and became the head of the KVM refugee task force. Do you recall approximately when you were appointed head of that task force in Albania?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been probably the third week of March. I'd been on leave when the actual withdrawal took place, then I rejoined my personnel in Macedonia, and then the refugee task force was created. So it was towards the end of March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why was this task force created? What was the purpose of this task force?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point there had been reports and, you know, obviously witnessing the pushing out of the personnel, the Kosovars, Albanians, who were being pushed out, some into Albania, some into Macedonia. Most of the KVM was regrouped in Macedonia, but there was a big issue with those that were coming into Albania, the -- many of the UN and NGOs, the UNHCR and NGOs were deployed in Albania, and were, you know, obviously sending reports and so forth. So there was a requirement, and they were looking for something for the OSCE to be able to support. We are a ready, if you wish, number of personnel that were kind of -- had been -- had been evacuated, and we also obviously had a bit of an emotional tie with Kosovo. So it was thought that we would put together a task force to go and assist the government of Albania with the refugees that were being pushed out from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to turn now to attachment 15 of -- it's tab 15 there in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, Exhibit P874 in our e-court system. We have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, and if yes, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It was produced by my -- by my personnel, the -- in the KVM refugee task force after we -- after we became officially effective in Albania. And the idea was that we were going to put together these bi-weekly reports specifically on human rights to be able to, kind of, assess and report on the situation as we saw it. And as you can see, this was for our internal use only, or at least a report that we were sending up to -- to the KVM headquarters on the situation as we saw it. So this was based on my verifiers who were deployed throughout Albania in each of the prefectures, the 12 prefectures. I was the only organisation that actually had people deployed right across the entire country, so I thought we could give a very good assessment, a good view of what we had witnessed and what we had in fact been able to interview from the different Albanians who were being pushed out into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the fact that you were conducting interviews with different Albanians who had been pushed out into Albania, and we also see that the document in the first line refers to the ongoing interviewing of refugees since 5th April. Were you personally involved in any of the interviews that were conducted with refugees that had been pushed out of Kosovo into Albania?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Because I wanted to see and experience what my verifiers were doing daily, of course I was on the ground continuously every day and in contact with refugees in different areas. I tried to go to a different area every single day. And, in fact, I took one statement, I did one interview myself during the -- that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us something about the accounts that you and your verifiers were hearing from the refugees that were coming into Albania from Kosovo? What sort of information were they providing you, recording what was going on in the province?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Generally the -- the types of statements that are in the -- in the record here, the human rights bi-weekly, were exactly the kinds of things that they were reporting. Reporting being pushed out, being forced from their homes often with just the things that they were able to carry; and at the border quite often having all their papers removed, being sometimes forced to give money. There were reports of killings and of raping and other activities, usually by the authority forces, usually in fact, by the MUP. And this kind of activity seemed to be a generalised -- a generalised activity that was going on at the time, and that was reported by the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the removal of papers, what sort of papers are you talking about that the refugees were speaking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring here to their identity papers so that when refugees came across they usually had no identity papers, nothing that could say where they were born, something -- nothing that could say where they were from originally, what they had worked at, any kinds of -- any kinds of those types of papers. And therefore, one of the activities that we were contemplating organising in the future was to do a kind of a registration programme where we would use some of the -- some of the colleagues and cooperators there such as the IOM and, you know, some private companies, in fact, to help us to put together a registration programme where we would create new identity documents for these people who had frankly, you know, no record of where they had been born, et cetera. So this was -- and what was also interesting is as we were -- as the refugee task force stood up, we had very bright orange vehicles and, of course, Kosovars had seen us patrolling throughout the area of Kosovo and so -- with these same vehicles. So when they came into Albania and would see bright orange vehicles, they usually were like a magnet and they would come up and start talking to the verifiers that were in there, including many of the local personnel who had been employees of the KVM in Kosovo. So those -- those employees had, you know, obviously, most of them could speak English. We were able to get, I think, good statements and truthful statements from them, so that was useful. So a lot of these -- a lot of these statements and a lot of these activities that they were reporting were able to be corroborated, you know, and able to be discussed at length with them. So including the lack of identity papers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you spoke to these persons about the lack of identity papers, what did they tell you had happened to them? How had they lost their identity papers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in fact, all of them said that they were -- these were taken away from them. They were searched, and they were taken away from them at the border when they were pushed across by the local authorities in Kosovo. And there were a couple of them who, you know, at their peril actually hid them inside their clothing very, you know -- in some areas that we won't mention here, but you know, that's -- some of them, actually, that's the only way they were able to actually bring out their papers. But most of them had their papers removed. You know, the authorities would ask to see the papers, they would look at them, and then keep them and just push them along. In fact, I don't know if I mentioned this already, but they often did that with their car licence, they would remove the car licence off the cars so the cars would come across with no licence plate. Nothing that would say the car came from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you understand was the significance of this, of the removal of identity cards and licence plates from the cars at the time when you were hearing these accounts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these accounts kind of, you know, obviously to me it seemed that we -- it seemed to be a way of the local authorities trying to push these people out to ensure they did not return since they had no papers saying they were originally from Kosovo. It would be pretty hard for them to return to their area of birth, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to one final document, and this is attachment 16 to your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. If we could have that up on the screen. This is Exhibit 875 now in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just wait until it's there; we have it in the system. Could you explain what this is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a -- this is a progress report that I decided to put together -- that my personnel put together for me to present to the OSCE, to the KVM. It was meant to be an internal, once again, report, and so it was meant to be a report that really was no holds barred, no politics involved, and telling it as it was; that would explain, was kind of an assessment of the situation as we saw it on that day. Because I actually left a couple of days later from the mission area myself, so I wanted to leave with a document that kind of at least tied all the loose ends together and explained the situation as we saw it. As you may have seen, there's an annex for each one of the 12 prefectures that tries to really give the specifics of the situation in each one of those prefectures, because the Albanian approach to the -- to the refugee situation was that they were bringing the refugees and spreading them out throughout the country, as opposed to Macedonia where they were keeping them fairly close to the border with Kosovo. As I said, the refugee task force, we were the only organisation that had personnel spread out throughout the entire mission area, so we were able to give a good snap-shot of the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn to page 7 of this document, and in the e-court system it's page 8 of the English and page 10 at the bottom in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see here under the heading "Refugee Statistics" that there are some number that is are provided, it says 420.000, and then there are different numbers of refugee estimates. Can you tell us what is this source of the numbers that are contained within this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the source is mainly from the government of Albania. Although we were able to every day attend the government of Albania's coordination meeting where, of course, all the NGOs, the UNHCR, and so on were in attendance; and including the NATO Albania force which had deployed a few weeks before. So we were able to get these numbers and really confirm them with all these other institutions. So that was -- but I'm sure that the main source were the government Albania's estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning our way now from the document, just one last question I wanted to clarify an issue you referred to yesterday when I was by asking about the difference in task between regular police units and Special Police units, you referred to an incident in Rogovo and you said you seen special police units in the aftermath of the incidents. I just wanted to know if you recall when that incident occurred in Rogovo and if you recall anything about that circumstance of that incident that you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- the Rogovo incident, if I remember, was, I believe towards the end of January, beginning of February. And it involved a group of, I think they were mostly KLA had crossed the border and come across and been followed, essentially, by the VJ, but I think took refuge in the city, in the little town of Rogovo in an enclave of a farm. And, I believe, at this point there was a MUP attack, and they actually caught the -- caught them red-handed, if you wish. But I think had been over a couple of days and the final kind of incident was in Rogovo itself. And a number of people, I think it was something like 25, were killed who, as I say, were mostly KLA in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Your Honour, you will be happy to know that I have no further questions at this stage for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have made my day, Ms. Kravetz. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic, do you cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a member of the Defence team for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic, assisted by Ms. Marie O'Leary, also a member of the Defence team. I have a few questions for you, and I will seek clarification of certain things that you said. I have read carefully and analysed all your statements and all the statements of people who used to be your associates, and in answering my questions, I would like you to distinguish between your personal knowledge and the knowledge of your underlings or perhaps superiors, because you did emphasise in your statement that you have certain knowledge which is not direct. I would like to ask you, first of all, about your brilliant military career. You joined the Canadian Armed Forces in the early 1970s, and in 1976 you graduated from the Royal Military College. Is that an equivalent of a military academy?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's a four-year course. Could you tell me what was your major at the academy?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in French literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm taken aback a little. You said it was a military academy, now you mention French literature, was your graduate paper in French literature?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, let me explain a little bit. The Canadian military academy, the Canadian Royal Military College is actually a military university and we, therefore, have -- we have all academic programs, engineering, arts, science; and the cadets that undergo the training there go to normal university except you go in uniform and you have military training outside of your academic pursuits. And so, in fact, it's based on four different components, the military components, academic, leadership, and athletic. So a graduate comes out with a full bachelor's degree, comes out with -- as a fully trained officer in the Canadian Forces, well fully trained, there's bit of more training required at the end, but also as a -- someone who can do some sports, and bilingual as well in French and English. My particular degree, university degree, if you wish, first degree -- first cycle was in French literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Now, when you graduated from the college, what rank did you receive?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a lieutenant in the -- and my military classification was in the armoured corps in tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This answers several of my questions. Since I am familiar with your career from your prior statements, I'd like to know -- I found somewhere that you were a company commander in France. Would you tell me what kind of organisation was it in France that you were a company leader, a company commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I was sent to France on exchange for two years when I was a young officer when both you and I had black hair probably at this point, and we -- I was the commander of a French conscript troop which, as you know France in those days had conscripts, they were doing -- they had service, military service for all -- for all personnel. And I was given command of a French conscript troop for 14 months out of the two years. Then I continued -- was promoted to captain and continued to serve there as an officer in -- a staff officer in the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By the way, we went to school at the same time, you and I, the same generation. I see that from 1994 you were chief of the administration of armoured forces and until 1998 you were chief of the administration of ground forces. Did you occupy that position until you left for Vienna?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I took over the position in February of 1998 and went to Vienna in November of 1998, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until you left for Vienna in November 1998, had you worked previously in any NATO agencies?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not. I had not worked in any NATO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps a liaison officer on behalf of the Canadian army cooperating with any NATO agencies, or did you have any other direct or indirect contact with NATO agencies?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, how come that from such a high position, you became a member of the Kosovo Verification Mission? Could you explain a little bit how that happened.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in I guess it would be the end of October 1998 -- first of all throughout my career I had had several UN deployments, and so I had been -- I had been outside the country on several occasions in different mission area, in Cyprus, also in the former Yugoslavia with the UNPROFOR, and I had also been on, as I said, on exchange in France, and I'd been working with the Americans a few times. I had a course -- by that time two course, sorry, in the United States. So I was fairly well versed, if you wish, in international operations. Towards the end of October, Canadian -- the Canadian Department of National Defence received word that -- it was kind of out of the blue -- of course, we had heard -- and the current situation in Kosovo was well in the news by then, and we had heard that there had been the agreement signed by Milosevic and Holbrooke in the middle of October, and I believe it was towards the end of October when we received a call from -- from the OSCE asking if we could provide a one-star, a brigadier-general level officer to become the head of the KVM support unit in Vienna. This was meant to be about a six-week deployment to Vienna only, and, you know, I was asked if I wanted to go and fulfill that mission. And so I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was almost a complete description of yourself, brigadier-general with prior experience. Did you have any combat experience at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. The peacekeeping missions I had been in were indeed -- certainly the Cyprus missions were peacekeeping missions that were, let's just say, quite stable; although there had been, you know, incidences of firing and so on. My first tour in the Balkans from 1993 to 1994 for one year as chief of operations, I had -- no, I had not been in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about after 1999, after you left the OSCE. Did you gain any combat experience?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just said that you had left for Vienna for a few weeks, but that turned out to be a few months. Did you stay within the OSCE, and what was the legal form of your engagement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did stay within the OSCE. What happened is when I deployed to Vienna, I was there for a few weeks, and at this point they were standing up the KVM per se on the ground in Kosovo. And they had decided that different nations would take command of the different -- the five regional centres. The first regional centre to open was the one in Prizren, Regional Centre 1, and they -- I guess someone thought that Canada should be offered the position and I would, because of my knowledge, of course, of the KVM support unit, I would be a good person to deploy onto the ground. So I came back to Canada for one week to get my kit, my equipment, and then I deployed directly into Kosovo. I believe I arrived on the 13th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know, General, did you sign a contract with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This was, I guess, it was looked at as a -- just a normal mission, and I don't recall signing a contract, no. I was provided by Canada as one of the members of the OSCE as a, you know, as a voluntary contribution, I guess you could call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then conclude that you were paid by the Canadian government for the duration of your mission to the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you then have obligations both to the Canadian government and to the OSCE at the same time while you were a verifier?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very good question, and it's an issue, of course, that everyone from any country who has served with any international organisation has this kind of a split; I won't say split personality, but split ethical dilemma. In my case, all my missions with the United Nations I tried to be the best United Nations officer I could, but obviously you come from your country and you have some, you know, you have some attachment, and it's not, you know, it's something that you -- that you feel strongly about. In the case of my deployment to Kosovo, working with the OSCE, which was my first time working with the OSCE, I felt a strong attachment to the OSCE as an organisation because I believed that they were a capable and useful organisation that could actually do a lot of good. I also felt a very strong attachment and a very, kind of, impartial approach to my mission in Kosovo. I felt a strong attachment to the people of Kosovo of all ethnic backgrounds, and I really tried to be, you know, to be impartial between the different parties there. To treat them all equally with dignity, and to in fact, you know, it's a documented fact that I really tried to look after the Serbian people in Kosovo because I felt that there was a real danger to them. There might be some back-lash if there had been a final agreement on the status of the province. So you are right, it was one of those things where if when you are in one of those missions, you have an attachment and you try to be an impartial and a good member of the organisation, the international organisation, but of course, you are Canadian. Certainly I can say that I never -- I never, you know, had -- was in a position where I felt I could not do justice to both those loyalties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was an exhaustive answer. A very detailed one. The state in whose army you were serving and gave an oath to serve faithfully was a member of NATO; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that organisation, the NATO of which Canada is a member state, did, without approval of the United Nations, commence an air-strike campaign against Yugoslavia on the 24th of March, 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the time when you were seconded to the OSCE until the 24th of March, you, in your loyalty, worked conscientiously and in good faith both for your government and for the organisation to which you were sent on mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I worked for the OSCE and tried be the best OSCE officer I could. But as I say, my loyalty to Canada, was, you know, it was never challenged in terms of the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, there was no conflict between these two loyalties. But on the 24th when you withdrew -- or rather, no, you were on leave, you were not there at the time. From that date, the 24th, Canada as a member state of NATO was at war with the FRY; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was actually a legal declaration of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How about de facto?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are getting beyond my knowledge and my abilities to actually, you know, state what kind of a -- what kind of state existed between the two. The point is that Canada did participate in the NATO campaign. At that time, as I said, I was still an OSCE employee. I happened to be on leave. And when I returned, I returned as an OSCE employee and carried on until the end of my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are on the subject of withdrawal. When did you go on leave in 1999? And when did you return? And where to, after that leave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was about the middle of March, so it was a few days before the withdrawal which I think took place on the 20th of March. I believe I left around the 15th of March, and I returned at the end of March or beginning of April. It might have been the 1st of April, something around there, and I returned to Ohrid in Macedonia where my verifiers had been gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that while you were on leave you did not only rest, you must have been in contact with the Chiefs of Staff of the Canadian army and probably with the Ministry of Defence too, in view of the situation in the world?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I was not. I was in Paris, and so I was indeed just resting, but obviously watching the news very carefully and knowing that I had a return flight, I was -- our return flights all came through Skopje anyway so I was going to be landing in Macedonia; and I had contact with my verifiers on the ground to make sure someone was going to pick me up when I arrived in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. When you arrived in Macedonia, and later in Albania, do you know approximately what were the NATO ground forces in Albania at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, I could not -- well, approximately I could probably say that I was aware that there was a -- there was a brigade that was near Skopje that was there -- a German brigade, I believe, that was there in case of the requirement to assist the OSCE in withdrawing from Kosovo. But I don't have the details, and I was not actually privy to the information even at the time of the deployment of the NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of March, the diplomatic part of the Kosovo Verification Mission moved to Macedonia and later to Albania, and the Verification Mission stayed there for a while in Macedonia and Albania. At that time there was a liaison officer between the KVM and NATO; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there had been a liaison even prior to that, but I do believe that did exist. I had no -- again, I had no contact with that liaison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you know Lieutenant-Colonel Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From what you know, what was his job within the KVM until the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he certainly -- he was need at the OSCE headquarters, in the KVM headquarters in Pristina, and I know he worked for General DZ. He was one, I believe, of the officers from the fusion centre, but I don't know exactly what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that he accompanied you at the time when you stood in for Mr. Drewienkiewicz as chief of operations for the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He accompanied me where? I mean, I remember him being in the headquarters, yes, I do, but accompanying me, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not mean that he accompanied you literally, but he was with you at meetings which you attending as DZ's deputy?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you explain to me the functions of the liaison officer between the KVM and NATO in Macedonia and Albania after the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I don't know what their function was, but I presume -- I would presume from my military experience that the function of a liaison is to ensure that both sides are aware of what the other's activities are. That's usually what a liaison officer does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It remains unclear to me who headed and ran the KVM in Macedonia after the 24th of March, 1999, and in Albania.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- well, that's quite clear to me. The entire time that I was with the KVM, I was under the command of Ambassador Walker, William Walker; the deputy head of mission for operations was General DZ, as you know. When I returned from my leave at the end of March, the command arrangements were exactly the same in Macedonia. The KVM was still there, and the command function was still working, so Ambassador Walker and General DZ were still part of the command chain. And in fact, that's who I received my orders from to set up, to organise, and to deploy the OSCE/KVM refugee task force into Albania. And when we deployed to Albania, I was the OSCE head of that KVM refugee task force. And I reported, again, to Ambassador Walker and to General DZ, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've come to that subject. Tell me, how did your mission end in May 1999? Did your tenure simply expire or what?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. In fact, I had been -- the commitment had been for six months, so from mid-November to mid-May was essentially six months; and as I left, I handed command over to my deputy, who happened to be another Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, when you extended your stay in the OSCE in end 1998 and when it was decided that you should be sent to RC 5, do you agree that -- sorry, RC 1, not RC 5, thank you. Do you agree that from the moment the UN resolution was adopted and the agreement was signed, which you verified, at least a month and a half elapsed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, for example, that the agreement was signed on the -- I think it was the 16th of October, and I deployed into -- into Kosovo, I believe it was the 12th or 13th of December. I don't know when the UN resolution was voted exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We have two UN resolutions and several agreements between the 16th and 25th of October, but in that time the KVM had not yet been established, had not yet started to work. But your predecessor was working on the ground already, it was the KDOM; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. My understanding of the KDOMs, was that they were more like bilateral arrangements between the Former Republic of Yugoslavia and different countries, and again I, you know, I'm kind of out of my depth here how, in fact, these were set up. But essentially, I saw it as these we were bilateral arrangements with different countries to have -- and with the EU, which also had a KDOM, I believe. So these had been -- these were arrangements, bilateral arrangements. When the final agreement, let's say, the agreement between Holbrooke and Milosevic was signed, I believe then that the -- within the agreement, if my recollection is right, the agreement actually said that the KVM would absorb the KDOMs when it deployed. So we would deploy, if you wish, on top of the KDOMs and absorb them into the KVM structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that your memory is perfect. I would like to go back to the following: In those documents, we have obligations on the part of the FRY as well as the position and role of KDOMs prior to KVM deployment. I believe it was the end of October when the dead-line was for the FRY to meet the conditions in the aforementioned agreement. If that did not happen, the NATO activation order was already put in place, and the air-strikes were expected to commence, should that happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I'm not -- you know, I'm not sure about that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm telling you this because when you arrived on the 15th of December and when asked about -- by the Prosecutor about the documents you receive and the deployment of troops, you said that you were not familiar with all the details. I'm now taking you back to the fact that KDOM, prior to your arrival, performed the tasks of the mission, and that you merely continued those tasks. That is to say, that there was a continuity between the two organisations and the various KDOMs being absorbed by the KVM; was that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the way I -- again, I'm a simple military man. The way I saw the difference between the two missions is that the KDOM, Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, versus the KVM, the Kosovo Verification Mission, the mission was slightly different. And here is the way, in my mind, I made the difference: To my mind the KDOMs were observer missions that would observe the situation on the ground without interfering. They would observe and report. They were diplomatic missions also meaning they were missions that probably had more diplomats than military personnel in them. Certainly that's way I saw it. When I deployed with the KVM, I saw the mission slightly differently. I saw of it more as a verification mission. Although we never got to that level, I saw that as our primary mission, i.e., to verify. To verify to me implies having an agreement in place, having a number of standards that you need to verify, i.e., numbers of troops, patrolling plans, you know, arrangements for different activities. And that the verifiers would be there and would verify. Also, I saw it as a verification of the human rights situation, i.e., where we would attempt to not just observe, but also confirm and also report and also, I guess I saw it more as an interference type mission, interventionist type mission, than the KDOM had been. This may not be the correct interpretation, but that's the way I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Regarding the functions of KDOM and KVM, I believe your interpretations are excellent. But between the point when the agreement was signed until the moment you took your functions over, the initial preconditions of compliance was supposed to be confirmed by KDOM and handed over to your mission, and that was one of the reasons why there were still no air-strikes on the 27th of October when the dead-line was for the FRY to comply with the agreement. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but it does make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. As far as your memory serves you, did you receive the archives of the UK and US KDOMs in your territory RC 1 once they were absorbed by the mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive archives, i.e., papers or, you know, former reports, et cetera. But I did take under -- under command, if you wish, I assumed command of the area, of the Pristina -- sorry, the Prizren -- the Prizren area. And when I arrived, there were, I would say, maybe 50 UK KDOM members and probably about 12 or 15, I think, US KDOM members that rolled into my organisation. They had kind of operated, if you wish -- certainly the UK on a shoe string, and I was able to actually, when I arrived, issue -- start really putting together some structure to the mission. And that's when I produced my guidance and so forth to try and, you know, solidify, if you wish, the mission at that time. But I did not receive any prior documents and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your prior verification experience probably required no further training of you before joining the KVM; am I correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your deputy in RC 1 was the UK KDOM head; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The RC 1, can you tell me which municipalities it encompassed? What was its area of responsibility, so to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to have a map it to show you, but it was basically the entire Prizren area, so I can't list them for you, but it was the Prizren area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We will move on, and in the meantime try to come up with an area of responsibility map. In any case, let's start with the coordination centres. You had a coordination centre in Orahovac, I believe, and another one in Prizren, and a third one in Suva Reka. Therefore we can conclude that these were the three municipalities included and that there was Dragas, Dragas municipality towards the border, which also fell within your area; that was the AOR of RC 5; am I correct.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: RC 1, but I think you're -- I think you're correct, the three CCs, the three coordination centres, were indeed the ones you've laid out, Orahovac, Suva Reka, and Prizren. And yes, I did cover also the border, and I think that was the Dragas region right in the south of the -- the point -- the south point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Pec and Djakovica were not within the area of RC 1; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess I'll be right again. RC 5 also encompassed the municipalities of Pristina and Urosevac? That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: In your area of responsibility within the AOR of RC 1, which MUP structures or organisation -- organisational part was within the given area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I could not put a number or a -- or a -- you know, the name to the structure, but when I dealt with the MUP for my area, I went to the Pristina -- to the Prizren headquarters of the MUP there, and I believe it was Colonel Vojnovic and Vukobrat were the two heads of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you were a soldier, whereas these men were policemen. In any case, RC 1 had a liaison officer with the police; who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a former policeman himself, UK man called Les House [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did each coordination centre also have a liaison officer for the police?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those liaison officers for the police from the coordination centres, did they report to RC 1, that is to say, to you as the main centre in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately, but they reported really to the coordination centre head. I had -- the three coordination centres each had a head, and the liaison officers reported to them, and then they reported all to me, if you wish. But I -- my approach was always to try and keep the -- to keep the -- each one of the issues the lowest possible. So if there was a small issue in a coordination centre that could be dealt with the coordination centre head and the liaison officer with the MUP in their area, they would do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the way information was passed onwards. Once you received those reports, you would collate them and send them on to Pristina where the seat of the KVM was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that General DZ was in charge of that part, the part that was in charge of KVM operations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within your area of responsibility, that is to say, RC 1, which military organisations and parts were present?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had elements of two brigades within my -- of the VJ within my area of responsibility, plus, of course, the MUP organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For the time being, I'm only interested in the military part. Can you tell me which were the two military units?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there was a -- one brigade that was based in Prizren, and the numbers are in the papers here, I can't remember what they are, but -- and there were also elements of the brigade from, I think, Urosevac that were in the Dulje heights, what happened to be just inside my area. That's why I say I had elements of two different brigades of VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you agree that the brigade that was stationed in Prizren was the 549th Motorised Brigade commanded by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was commanded by General Delic. As for the number, I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the other part of the Urosevac brigade, was the 243rd Mechanised Brigade headed by Colonel Jevic; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Staying with that, there was only one part of that brigade at the Dulje heights with some of their elements falling within your area of responsibility; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In keeping with the agreement, one of the three roads along which the military could deploy a company was between Pristina and Prizren, or rather, between Stimlje and Suva Reka via Dulje; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again this is -- now my recollection is not so good, but I would take your word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to the documents showing that. I thought this may have been a quicker way to deal with it though. I'm asking you this because there were some parts of that brigade in the territory of RC 1, whereas some of its elements were in the area of RC 5; hence, the length of the road was split between the two centres. In any case, we'll see some documents showing that. General, I see that you attended several meetings with Colonel Delic and Colonel Jelic on one occasion. Who was the main liaison officer for the military within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to refer to my notes with -- for his name, but there was, indeed, a liaison officer with each of the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We needn't know his name, as long as we know he existed. How come you knew the entire military structure within your area of responsibility and at the same time you say you were not familiar with the MUP organisation there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good question, and probably related to the fact that I very easily associate with military structures such as brigades, but not so easily with paramilitary like the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This brings us to the third element, which is the KLA. Can you tell me which KLA operational zone was within your RC 1 area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the name of it exactly, but I -- from what I understood when I dealt with the -- the zone commander, his zone essentially covered as -- pretty close to the entire Prizren area, and I called with -- I dealt with this -- Drini was my usual contact there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your memory serves you correctly. It is interesting, though, that the entire operational zone of the KLA coincided precisely with the AOR of RC 1: Orahovac, Suva Reka, Prizren and Dragas. Was that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was so, and -- but I believe that, you know, the different municipalities like the regional centre from the OSCE's point of view was meant to cover the one-fifth of the territory, and I don't know what you call it, the province, I guess, within the province of Kosovo. So it seemed that certainly that that was the idea of the OSCE to give a -- not a municipality, but a number of municipalities to cover an area that had a prefect, et cetera, et cetera, you know, that fit within that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me put that to you again. The area of SUP Prizren also coincided with the area of responsibility of RC 1 covering the same municipalities and the same area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I also wanted to ask you about the departments of the interior which existed as a lower organisational level than the police stations, but this may not be so important at this point. Did you hear of the operational zone of the KLA was called Pastrik, the one that was within your area of responsibility and during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I subsequently heard that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Djakovica municipality as well as Pec municipality were outside your area of responsibility, as we have established. I'm now interested in another thing: Do you know what was the name of the operational zone where the 243rd mechanised brigade had its headquarters in Urosevac, Kacanik, and Stimlje; do you know what was that operational zone of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was the name of the operational zone headed by Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know the name of the operational zone, but I understand that this was the one that included Pec and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We have discussed the three organisations. On top of, that you also communicated with civilian authorities. You said that the person in charge of that area was Ms. Branka Furijanovic, which is correct. On several occasions in your statement you said that the Chief of SUP Mr. Vojnovic was the prefect deputy, I'm interested to find out where did you learn of that information? Where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall where I got it from, but certainly it was not me who actually, you know, found out, I don't think. I think I was told that by one of my -- one of my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to reporting. All information that you received at the level of RC 1, you sent to the KVM in Pristina. In what format?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would have been a daily sitrep format, situation report. And I had taken the habit of -- my staff, first of all, my operation staff would take the reports from each the coordination centres and put them to the format of the report that we would sends to the KVM. But I had taken the habit - when I was in the headquarters, and when I wasn't there my deputy did it - of trying to provide a general assessment at the last part of each one of those daily sitreps. So probably about 10.00 at night I would come in and read the sitrep, and because I had been in the area during the day, I had a sense of the atmosphere and what was going on. So I would try to really give a commander's view of the day's activity, the day's kind of atmosphere, context, environment, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand correctly that all important events were registered and that the seat of the mission was informed of those? On top of that, you also provided your comments and your view of those events?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know this: Was the reporting done in written form and sent by fax messages or courier, or was it via telephone, or both?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by fax. It was sent and faxed to KVM headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you keep copies of those reports at the RC 1?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your archives, once the KVM and RC 1 left the FRY, did you take that to Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the same thing was done by the seat in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All of these important things we have been discussing were contained in your daily reports; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, according to what I know about the KVM, you were all answerable to Ambassador Walker who was the head of mission, and he was the only person authorised to issue official statements and positions as the various events in the field were concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you stood in for General DZ, and given that you were familiar with the relationship with the FRY authorities, did you know that at the level of the FRY, there was a federal commission for cooperation with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know now. I don't know -- I'm not sure if I knew while I was on the ground in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We have a few minutes left before the break. Can you tell me what information did you have about that while you were in Pristina and before you went away on the 20th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anyone ever told me there is a commission that is in charge of liaison with the KVM, et cetera, et cetera. But I did, of course, meet Mr. Sainovic, and I met with General Loncar's deputy while I was there once, at least on one occasion, might have been, in fact, two. So -- but I didn't know that the structure was actually called a commission or a liaison office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I think it's time for the break. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic, we will have our first break now. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I have looked through my preparation papers, and I found a note that you stood in for DZ from 28th December, 1998, until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down with the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- that you stood in for him on three occasions. And that meeting where you said you were with Mr. Keller and Mr. Sainovic, that was on the 6th of January, 1999. It was such an uninteresting meeting that I did not take the document to show it to you, but we did use it as an exhibit earlier. The discussion was about some helicopters, the KVM requested helicopters that were to be painted over and used for transport to Macedonia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I don't remember, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, we'll move on. I'd like to ask you one more thing about the organisation of the KVM. Mr. Walker had several deputies covering different areas, one was more operation, that was General DZ; but I also found a note that the deputy chief of mission for the police was Giovanni Kessler; do you remember that man?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him. I probably, you know, had some contact with him, but I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Never mind. I'm interested in the relationship between RC, as the territorial unit of the KVM, and this deputy chief mission for the police. Did you have any obligation to report to him separately about the police aspects of your contacts in your area of responsibility or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up Exhibit P857, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, there it is. Do you agree that this was the area of responsibility of RC 1 which you headed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm what we have discussed so far, that the image here corresponds to your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this drawing as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. I'm told it's already part of Exhibit P857. The system has got ahead of us, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it is part of an exhibit, page 4, but I thought that since this was a confirmation of the witness's testimony, this is a sketch of the territory. If it is superfluous, I accept that. And now I'd like to call for Exhibit D160.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I'll now move on to documents that served as a basis for verification. While we are waiting for this document to be shown on the screen, were you familiar with Resolution 1199 with the agreement Geremek-Jovanovic, the agreement Byrnes-Djordjevic, and the agreement Clark-Naumann, Sainovic-Djordjevic? Those were the four documents that served as a basis for verification.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the time certainly aware of them and quite familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think you even made an analysis of the obligations and the work of RC 1 based on these documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In fact, my guidance to my verifiers uses those documents as the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up page 3, para 4, and I'd like subparagraph (a).

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I want to discuss with you certain passages from this resolution. Obligations of Yugoslavia, (a): "To cease all action by the security forces affecting the civilian population on order the withdrawal of security units used for civilian repression." Is it correct that this provision does not apply to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe those are -- those are FRY obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in (b) and (c) we read obligations of the verification to enable movement and monitoring, the obligation of dialogue; and now in paragraph 5 (b) another obligation is: "Not to carry out any repressive actions against the peaceful population." Only the peaceful population, that's the translation I have and I believe it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I see on my screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is no obligation here not to take any steps against the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, if they are peaceful, I guess there's an obligation not to take any action against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And if they are not peaceful, there is no ban on measures against them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I read it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up P836.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an understanding between Mr. Byrnes and Mr. Djordjevic regarding observation points. I believe that under item 5, Stimlje-Dulje, a total of six observation points are envisaged; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I see on my screen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your area of responsibility, part of Stimlje-Dulje is included; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You know that area very well, that area of responsibility of yours was up to the border between municipalities Urosevac and Suva Reka; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, when you go from Stimlje, just before the top is the border between Urosevac and Suva Reka; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been there for more than ten years now, but I believe that that's about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking all this not to test your knowledge, far from it. I just want to know how many observation points were in your area of responsibility, the RC 1?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a question I can't answer. I cannot remember, and I don't even think that we ever got to the point where we were able to identify exactly how many observation points were in any of my area. And again, I believe that was a result of the fact that we never received the specific verification standards that I was mentioning earlier that we were hoping at some point to receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we have an exhibit in this case, P844 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for your reference, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's a chronology of the main events from the 15th October, 1998, until 18th of April, 1999. It's a document created by General DZ as chief of operations. In this document under -- I'm sorry about this noise. Items 57 and 58, it is stated in 58 that an inspection was carried out of 27 observation points on the 5th of January. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that on the 4th of January combat positions of combat teams were inspected? That's page B-3 in English. You see it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. In fact, I believe that I was involved in those inspections with Colonel Kotur where we were able to go visit the three -- the three VJ positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And in your area of responsibility, if you toured VJ positions, there was only one. We'll reach that document later. Very well. Thank you. Just while we still have this document in front of us, Shaun Byrnes and Djordjevic, do you agree that -- or do you know that this agreement was implemented prior to your arrival, P836. I believe you have it. It's your document. It covers these observation points.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It was signed, I think, on the 25th of October, so this was before I got there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up P835. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at para 3. General, would I be right in saying that this paragraph 3 does not apply to traffic check-points and points erected for purposes of crime control? That's the translation I've got.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, they are actually quite specific here. They are saying for purposes other than traffic or crime control, so that would be a correct interpretation on your part, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were on the ground, did you see those traffic check-points and placements created to check whether there was any arms or drug smuggling or other substances that were banned?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times. Now, as for the reasons why these check-points were there, this could be the reason that the authorities believed that they needed to have these check-points. But in my particular -- in my personal view, some of them were unnecessary and actually stopping too many vehicles in many instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that all the vehicles that moved on the road were stopped and checked except, of course, your vehicles which had immunity?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move to paragraph 4 of this document. It deals with the issue of verification and border control. Would you agree with me that throughout the tenure of the mission, there was a dispute between the mission and the FRY authorities about how border control and verification of the border were affected?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say -- I would not say there was a disagreement. There was a difference of opinion as to the freedom of movement of the KVM in the border area and the way the FRY authorities saw that same freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You as a diplomat phrased it much better than I would. Now, let me ask you, considering this difference of opinion, were you aware that this difference of opinion between the verification mission and the commission of the federal government was raised to a higher level? Was the president of OSCE informed, and did he discuss it with the authorities of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in the right place vis-a-vis the border, General. This difference of opinion concerned the border belt. One treatment applied to the border belt which had a depth of 5 kilometres, and another treatment applied to the area beyond 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a frequent subject of discussion between the authorities and myself as to, you know, I felt that I was -- I wanted to go and see, verify, observe activities along the border, visit the villages that were within the 5 kilometre area; and often was unable to do so because the authorities always required me to have a liaison officer accompany me. And quite often, they had no liaison officers available, et cetera, et cetera. So this was a regular source of -- a regular issue that came up with the authorities and the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. We have a record of your conversation with Colonel Delic about the stations in Planeja and notices of verification. But the point was that within this border belt, the 5 kilometres, the military authorities required prior notice subject to approval; and you believed that could you come to that border belt 5 kilometres unannounced and conduct inspections?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now call up P837, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the Clark-Naumann-Sainovic Agreement, and Djordjevic. What is important in my view is what is one part of this document that pertains to the FRY government communique which took over the responsibility of implementing it. At page 2, item 2, of the statement, am I right in saying that the FRY took on the obligation to reduce the staffing strength of the MUP and army to the level which existed before the terrorist activities commenced?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the next page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, item 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Court Clerk, you don't need to put the B/C/S on the screen; the English will suffice since I have a paper copy for my testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, in item 5, we see that three check-points are referred to, or three locations at which the VJ had the right to deploy a company per location in order to protect the traffic and the road?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember that the agreement concluded that the company should number 100 to 120 men including -- plus their equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we understood to be a company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under (c) of this item do you see the mention of the road Prizren-Suva Reka-Pristina which fell partly within the area of responsibility of RC 1 that you were head of?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, that company was at Dulje, was that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next look at item 7. Having read the agreement, did you notice item 7 back in 1998 when you probably saw it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the FRY undertook to comply with the obligations by 1200 hours on the 27th of October pertaining to the agreement, and the other part of the item mentions that line of 1200 hours on the 29th of October?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this article, KDOM was supposed to monitor these withdrawals; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Some of it even spills over into item 4, but in any case, I wanted to ask you this: Do you recall that NATO, or rather, Mr. Javier Solana had an activation order in place should there be a non-compliance on the part of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm -- I don't recall, but it's probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There was no bombing, that is not in dispute, but that was avoided precisely because the FRY met its obligations envisaged in the documents, in which we can see that the legal predecessor of KVM was KDOM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
