utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you succeeded KDOM, and when I say "you," I mean the KVM; and you took over their work in keeping with the contents of the verification agreements; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From your answer, I gather that you were not familiar with the previous compliance of the FRY that had been verified by KDOM once you resumed that work first in Pristina and then as head of RC 1, you were not familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I was familiar, and in fact, I knew that the company position in Dulje heights was an approved and agreed position that was allowed to be in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was your area of responsibility. There were several obligations that were undertaken, that, for example, 10.000 policemen would be left in Kosovo, that all soldiers be returned to the barracks, and that all units that had been deployed to Kosovo before February, as well as all police units, be returned to Serbia. There were several obligations to be met; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Roman numeral III, last sentence, please have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, the conclusion of para 3, does it authorise FRY authorities to respond to terrorist activities adequately and proportionately exercising self-defence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and to me the operative words are "adequately" and "proportionately."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will discuss that a bit later. I'm, for the time being, interested in the right to act against terrorists. Thank you, General. Speaking of adequacy and proportionality, as a senior military expert, having in mind the time that elapsed since your last verification mission and today, has your position changed on the principal of adequately and proportionately using force?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. As I mentioned yesterday, I believe, in my testimony, the pattern that we often saw happening was that the response would be disproportionately great by the authorities when some of the incidents were, I don't want to say minor, but were of a smaller nature. So the reaction was usually disproportionately greater than the incident itself. And I guess what has changed, of course on the basis of what is happening now in Afghanistan, in these counterinsurgencies throughout the world, we see quite often the need for proportional response with respect to the size of forces. And, I mean, could go into it in a lot more detail, but I don't think it's worth doing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to discuss the criteria. I don't know whether you saw the news on the BBC yesterday, I heard that in Pakistan, three and a half million civilians left their homes because of the alliance -- allied forces operation. That thousands of people were killed, and that 200 million dollars were earmarked by the US government to aid Pakistan, to deal with the consequences of this operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the news, but it's quite possible that that's the case. I know there's a major activity going on in the Swat valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you believe, do you think, that this represents a proportion at use of force resulting in the removal of three and a half million people and 3.000 people being killed, and then let's talk about cluster bombs and depleted uranium ammunition, does that constitute proportionality?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to you, since you are the expert in terms of the territory where you were, would you agree with me that the conflicts and the incidents which took place during your mandate there, for the most part happened in the country-side in rural areas?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On occasion they were in the country-side, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When I say rural or outside urban areas, I mean the smaller towns ending with villages. But for me, Racak is no town nor is Randubrava. Since you visited those places, can you tell me what does a typical Albanian home look like in those village? What does it's yard look like? And what possibility does one have to access the house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. These houses are, indeed, they are not built up areas such as, you know, in the middle of Prizren, for example. They are not apartments. They are usually houses that are dislocated and, for example, in Rogovo, there was a number of small houses that were joined together by a fence, kind of in an open area, kind of a yard where you could come in. It was kind of a farm-type conglomeration of houses. So that was more typical of the -- of Albanian housing in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These yards were behind tall walls which contained a gate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that such structures, if used for military purposes, represent well-fortified or well-protected facilities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you something else that you are also an expert in. What is the proportion or relationship between the attacker and the one defending for the attacker to be able to win?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The common planning figure is three to one. Three attackers to one defender.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about technical means?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, in terms of overwhelming force, in terms of?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What you told me in your answer has to do with soldiers. What about the technical means, equipment, or assets that would be needed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in a normal attack, say, when we were, you know, in my staff college days, we would try to have as many of the weapons available to us, available to put on a particular attack. Now, it depends, of course, at what level you are talking about. When you are talking about a divisional or brigade level, you usually are talking about some important and large weapons. When you are talking about small -- small section attacks, then we are talking about small-arms weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to ask you this: If we have a village which such houses containing 10, 20, or 30 enemy, wouldn't it be normal then, and expected, to have a company to clear the area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you believe that many legal representatives of authorities need to be killed in order to liberate an area that was taken up by terrorists?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. To go back to the time preceding your stay in Kosovo, you must have heard that after the agreement that was met in full by the FRY by pulling out its army and police forces, taking them outside of Kosovo, returning them to the barracks, that the KLA used that to expand their territory and take up positions in the locations from which the FRY forces had been withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since your area of responsibility also included the border, and there were some incidents there, would I be right in saying that across that border contrary to the UN resolutions there was constant arms smuggling from Albania for the benefit of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the KVM notified the OSCE on the violations of the resolutions by the KLA -- or by Albania?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the Security Council of the UN informed of Albania as the state contributing actively to the arming of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the OSCE or the UN were apprised of the issue. Certainly in my area whenever we had evidence of arms smuggling and so on, we would certainly advise the KVM headquarters. As a matter of fact, I think as you know, when I arrived in Kosovo in December, there had just been an incident where a number of people were killed by the border guards, border security guards, and they certainly seemed to be people of fighting age.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe it was also your assessment that it was KLA who were trying to enter illegally smuggling arms, and that they were encountered by the representatives of authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, looking at the chronology of events between the 15th of October and the 18th of April, 1999, one would not gain the impression that in your area of RC 1 there were grave problems that were caused by FRY authorities, and that any of such events were reported to the operations department.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether there were many or not many. Certainly I had -- I had, I think, a pretty good grip on events that were going on, and we had indeed good relations generally with the authorities and with the KLA; so we were able, I think, to keep events and incidents to the minimum.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you have testified about Racak and Rogovo, both of which fell outside your area of responsibility; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Racak for sure. Rogovo I think was right on the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were at a meeting with Mr. Vojnovic. In any case, Rogovo is Djakovica municipality rather than Prizren; you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'd like to move on to some of your documents and some meetings where you attended. The first thing I'd like to know is something that has to do with Exhibit P854. General, this is a note on the handover dated the 5th of December, 1998, I think this is your report or information sheet that you left to your successor; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the wrong document on my screen, but I do believe that that is the one you are referring to. When I was at the KVM support unit and left those notes for my successor on the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misstated the number. The exhibit is P854. While waiting for it, we can continue discussing this subject. That was in the period while you were still not the head of RC 1. I wanted to read something out. In item 3, you say: "During one of your trips to Skopje, you should visit the KVM C and meet with Brigadier David Montgomery. Commander of the KVCC which is of essential importance to analyse air and land information."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if the document could be displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's trying to be located, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was page 19, 65 ter number 2772, and page 18 in the English. Could we please confirm the information Ms. O'Leary provided me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, let us not waste any time since you have to travel tomorrow, I believe. I'd like to give you my hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And of item 3, the last sentence. I wanted to ask you for your explanation of the acronym KVCC and what is this essential coordination to verify air and land information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KVCC was an organisation that had been set up in Skopje, and I believe it was as a result of the first -- the first agreements between the FRY and the OSCE and the FRY and the UN, et cetera. The KVCC I believe was there to coordinate particularly air forces, in the case of, as you said, an air campaign in Kosovo. I believe that that is what the KVCC was. So for us, it was important to, as we were standing up, the Kosovo Verification Mission, that we have at least the head of the support unit in Vienna have visited there, and I thought it was a critical activity that he needed to undertake, and that's why I suggested that he visit this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Am I right in saying this: Pursuant to the Clark-Perisic [as interpreted] Agreement, I believe, air verification was to be done by NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when there is a mention of coordination, it has to do with the collation of both land and air data?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Given that you are an expert in that, when there is air surveillance in place, can't you see any movements of troops? For example, on Google, I can follow what is going on right now in Ottawa?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is a possibility to be able to observe. The issue is, of course, how time sensitive is it, and I think unless you have persistent observation, it's very difficult to actually tell movement of troops. And it also depends on the cover from the air, et cetera, et cetera. There's a whole bunch of technical issues to that. But generally, the idea is to ensure that you are coordinating the land -- ground verification and air verification. Usually what can happen is the air verification can take place with the confirmation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that FRY forces used roads, and they were easy to observe wherever they were, and they were easy to follow?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not really agree with you that they would be easy to observe. Those that are on the roads, of course, are easy to observe. But, you know, there's -- as a military man, I know you can hide pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But with your mobile patrols, as far as I heard, you changed the method of verification, you wrote down the numbers of vehicles of the FRY and gradually established their bases, their movements, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we were able to observe movement and so on, my verifiers actually did as much reporting as they could in terms of details, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does the name Donna Phelan ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Ms. O'Leary was right about the number of the exhibit, she just did not mention page 4. Can I now call up again -- it's again 854, but we'll come to that later. Let's take 860.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is about your 26 December, 1998 meeting with Colonel Delic. What I'd like to know here is on page 3, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can just scroll down a little -- sorry, scroll down. I don't need the signature, go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel Delic tells you the normal procedure here is for teams going into the field to announce themselves to the Major at 4.00, or to give four hours notice where and when they are going because we are answerable for their safety.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We've already discussed this, General, so I won't dwell on it. I'd just like to ask you: Are you aware that sometime on the 15th of March discussions started and it was agreed that you, the verifiers, may enter territories engulfed in the fighting at your own peril; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, about the installation of your mission in the border belt and in Planeja village. Didn't Colonel Delic say that he was not authorised to decide about that, that only the superior command could decide?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now have P864, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is your conversation on the 16th of January with Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic from the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. I'd like to know one thing: Where does it say that the army may not conduct training outside barracks? In which document would we find that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in one of the previous documents that you showed me, this was only allowed with prior coordination with the KVM. This was in one of the agreements, I don't recall which one, but that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll now read out to you something on page 2, item 1, in the B/C/S version. I don't know if I'll be able to find the English reference. It must be on the first page. It says: "P," that must be Petrovic. "We received authorisation for these tasks." Did Petrovic inform you that these drills outside the barracks were authorised, allowed? The second part of the sentence is: "My commander is coming back Sunday night."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me here, and I understand what you are saying. This is what Petrovic was saying that night that they had been authorised. But as you know, I was at that meeting with Gil Gilbertson who was the deputy head of the RC from RC 5, and he was confirming to me that they had not had authorisation to move from the barracks, and that they had been, indeed, at the time deployed for several days outside. And that's why I was saying to them that it was an unauthorised [Realtime transcript read in error "authorised"] move and it was -- and that they were ready to fire towards Dulje, et cetera, and trying to find out what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Maybe Gilbertson told you that, I don't know when, but we don't have his response, his reaction to this statement by Mr. Petrovic. Your meeting -- that meeting was at 10.37 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it right that Mr. Gilbertson did not react to this statement by Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask, General, if you look on the screen in front of you, page 55, line 11, it suggests that at the end there that it was an authorised move, if you can pick up the line.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: An unauthorized, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's what you said, yes. Thank you. So that line 11 needs to be unauthorised, not authorised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am not in a position to follow the transcript at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On this document, one more thing: Below the point you were looking at, there's another one where again Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic says: "The KLA provoked an attack on MUP in Dulje heights, problems in Javor and Luznica, but to the best of my knowledge, no fire from tanks on 14th of January occurred."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see where that is, yes. Is he referring there, of course, to the ambush by the KLA of the MUP convoy, I believe took place on the 8th of January; so a few days before this meeting, that's what he is referring to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But he also mentions there was no fire on the 14th of January?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did mention that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P869.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll move on, General, to the incident in Racak of the 15th January. It's right, isn't it, that Racak is not in the area of responsibility of RC 1, is it correct that on the 15th of January, you were at a meeting in Pec with General Drewienkiewicz and other chiefs of regional centres?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after your luncheon, you received the first information about something that happened in Racak, and at DZ's request, you set out towards Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind how long it takes to travel from Pec to Racak and the time when you set out, you arrived at dark; and the only contact you had was in Stimlje concerning some people who were wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Later on, going through some documents that you created, we'll look at some more details. Is it the case that on the 16th of January, 1999, when DZ and General Walker arrived, the bodies were moved to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Ambassador Walker. I believe that some of the bodies were moved to the mosque, but many of them were still in Racak, particularly in the -- in the ravine area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. I got what I just said from the witness statement of General DZ that at that time when he came, together with Ambassador Walker and yourself, the bodies were moved to the mosque. But let me ask you this: Is it the case that Racak was not under the control of the FRY forces from the afternoon of the 15th until the time when you arrived on the 16th January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you define "under the control" by meaning that there was no authority presence in Racak, I believe you would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if you know this, but the -- you must have found out later, the on-site investigation by FRY authorities was carried out only on the 17th of January after failed attempts on the 15th and the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm well aware. In fact, I was on the ground on the morning of the 17th when the investigation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Am I right in saying that at the time when Ambassador Walker -- but he is also a general, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. I thought he was. But never mind, he was certainly an ambassador. When Ambassador Walker and General DZ were there, the local KLA commander was also in Racak and on the 16th Ambassador Walker spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And is it right that not a single person who perished in Racak was killed from heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my -- that would be my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you this one, because I know you did not see that, but let me ask you something else. You saw the terrain around Racak and the high ground on which you stood, you say in your statement you did not see any casings around trenches?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, General, you said yourself you were not an expert in ballistics, but as a military man; if there are no casings around the bodies, that means that they were hit from a great distance; is that right? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, either that or the casings were picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it's the KLA that had control over the site, not the FRY authorities. But let's move on. Since there were trenches there and the persons who were a party to the conflict were in trenches, wouldn't it be logical that in the case of a skirmish, any wounds would be to the head, or at least the upper part of the body?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Milosevic asked me that question about seven years ago, and my answer was the same as it is now, and that is that when we learn how to shoot, we always aim for the centre of mass. We never aim for a particular part of the body, we aim for the centre of mass, that's the best way to ensure that the soldier hits the target. So in this case, obviously if there's only part of the body that's exposed, the centre of mass would be that, you know, the centre of that part of the body that is exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's the rule of the bull's-eye on the chest in target practice. Have you ever seen the video made by the Verification Mission when they were there in Racak on the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I've seen it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you see in the course of trials and court proceedings any report by your verifiers from RC 1 or RC 5 about the Racak incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean out of this court? I believe I -- I believe I've only seen what I have in my depositions, et cetera. I don't think I've seen anything from any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I just said reports by verifiers, you were at too high a level and you just summed up the reports of your subordinates. You sent your own report on the 16th and the 17th. Were you shown any reports by individual verifiers in this case, in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall if I was shown any in this courtroom, but I can tell you that on the ground, before preparing my own reports, et cetera, I may not have seen any written reports by my verifiers, but I certainly talked to all of them that were there, and I kept in very close contact. And so I developed my assessments based on my discussions with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please focus on my question. I asked you about yesterday and earlier today. Did you see any such document created by one of your verifiers, or verifiers from RC 5?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told me that the complete archives of the OSCE were moved from Pristina, that is the regional centres, to Macedonia and Albania; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I said that; I'm not sure they were. I know that I took my personal archives such as the sitreps, et cetera, through my deployment further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are right. You were talking about yourself, not the entire mission. Now, General, were you aware, at the time or later, that Stimlje, Racak, and Urosevac were within the Nerodimlje operation zone of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the name of the operation zone, I knew it was outside of my, I'll just say, the commander of my operational zone within my area. I knew it was outside of his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Excellent. You've anticipated my next question. When you spoke to Mr. Drini, you spoke about the area that was not in his territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, knowing that it was not in his territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, after so much discussion about Racak, would I be right in saying that in Racak itself and the environs, KLA members were present on the 15th when the operation in Racak began?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would be right. I never had any contact with them myself in Racak or Stimlje, but my verifies indeed did have some contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One more thing, the KLA also confirmed that a certain number of their members were killed in Racak, but let's put that aside. When you talked to Mr. Drini - I believe it was, on the 17th of January, 1999 - he told you that the wounded members of the KLA, a number of them, were placed in hospitals that he had on his territory and his area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. It's probably in the record of meetings, but I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 869, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To finish with the meeting you had with the chief of SUP Urosevac, Mr. Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You'll agree with me, General, that unlike the conversation with Mr. Petrovic where you were involved in the discussion, this time it was Mr. Gilbertson who took the chair and you made just a few remarks; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We had agreed that that would be the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it right that Mr. Janicevic briefed you on the situation including the events in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he gave us his account.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: His account. But since it was not your territorial responsibility, you did know that on the 8th of January in Sljivovo -- or rather, you didn't know that a police patrol was attacked in Sljivovo on the 8th of January, you didn't know about the kidnappings of Albanians in that area, it was not your area, and did you not have any prior knowledge of these things; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we look at page 2; I believe it's page 2 in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, General, that the chief of SUP told you that the action was approved by the staff, and he led about 100 policemen who took part?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did tell me, indeed, that he was in charge of the 100 policemen, and I don't know what you mean about that this was an agreed -- oh, you are probably referring to the part where he talks about Article 3 being fulfilled, is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And here we see the line where he tells you, Even at the position of chief of the police, we cannot make final decisions, it's the staff that has to decide because they issued the order. Is this a correct interpretation, a correct account of your discussion?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to assist, I believe the passage my learned colleague is referring to is at page 7 of the English. This document has three versions and the operative one is the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That may assist to find the correct page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've lost sight of the question. Would you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You've seen the document. I asked you two things at the same time. One, that this chief of the police told you that it was the staff that approved the operation and issued the orders; and two, that he led the 100 policemen who carried out the operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's time for the break, General, but just one brief question: Is it correct that Mr. Janicevic denied at this meeting that any members of the Army of Yugoslavia participated in the action?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, General. I believe it's time for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the second break now. And we resume at 1.00. You are on target for time, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have decided so, and that's how it will be. And I would like to thank the General who is giving me very brief and very precise answers. I hope he will keep up in the same vein. And then at the end, I'll have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, were you aware, at the time when you were a part of the Verification Mission in Kosovo, that the KLA had 60 millimetre mortars and 80 millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had been reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In this document that should be in front of you, I see that Mr. Janicevic also told you at this meeting of the 16th of January, that the KLA did use the 60 millimetre mortar and the 80 millimetre mortar; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't see it on my -- on my record of meeting here, but I believe that they did indeed mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's on the first page of the record. In your Regional Centre 1, you had a certain David Wilson; do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He was the liaison officer with the KLA for your regional centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, he was the chief liaison, so the liaison officer for the KLA and the liaison officer for the authorities reported to him as the chief of the liaison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that he attended the conference in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because I sent him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us then about his mandate in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Rambouillet to actually keep us informed of the progression of the negotiations. The idea was that the KVM had -- I had suggested to General DZ that KVM should be represented there to get a sense of what was going on and so his mandate was, if you wish, I had loaned him to KVM headquarters, and his mandate was to report back on the progression of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he help the delegation of the Kosovar Albanians during the conference?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: May I ask you now if it is the same David Wilson --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document 65 ter 641.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you will see that this is a report by David Wilson of 15th March, 1999. Evaluation of KLA positions on the 15th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, is that the David Wilson you had on your team?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's the same one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In sub-item (d), do you remember that on the 14th of March, the KLA renewed its attack, its ambush attack in Dulje?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can I call up P870. Sorry, I don't need that one. We don't have time for it. P872.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a meeting of the 17th January, 1999, you had with Mr. Drini. Let me just draw your attention to bullet point 8 from the top. "D" means "Drini." Speaking of exposure to special fire, he spoke of the need to acquire indirect fire weapons, maybe Katyusha rockets?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us any details about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. Actually, it happened quite often that there was a lot of bluster from the KLA about how they were going to get these weapons and these weapons and this came totally from left field. I was very surprised, and as you can see, I don't think it was brought up again this that meeting or subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at line 5.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's in between quotation marks here, it says: "Some were released, some are in serious condition and still in my hospital." And he was talking about the wounded from Racak and Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And that should be in "military" hospital. M-i-l is, certainly in the English, in the original, means "military," in military hospital, which I was not aware there were KLA military hospitals, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of this document, please look at point 4 and give us your comment. While you are reading, let me read it out: "We are going to continue talking to US KDOM, although they are cowboys, they can get the job done with their bulldozer policy." "Bulldozer." Tell me, what did Mr. Drini tell you about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the issues was that within my zone, my regional centre, I often received reports that there was -- that the US KDOM, those portions that had not integrated into my regional centre, were operating. And I found that frustrating at times because of course they would meet with different parties, and I was not aware of the subjects of those meetings or the reports or what had been decided, et cetera. So this was, for me, a bit frustrating, and I was then talking to Drini about this and saying that, you know, I found it frustrating and that's the point at which he said that he would continue to talk to the US KDOM for that -- for the reason, I guess, that he has got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But I want to know what this meant: "They can get the job done with their bulldozer policy." What was it that he told you that prompted the person who made this record to write something like this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Drini said exactly that, is that he would continue to talk to the US KDOM because in his view even though they were not as controlled as we in the OSCE were, that, of course, they had the political weight of the United States and therefore presumably would continue to get the job done. I didn't know what job he was speaking about, but all I know is that I found it very frustrating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Perhaps I don't need to show you a document, but I'd like to ask you whether the KLA was against you establishing a station in Planeja?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the KLA was against? I am not sure whether the KLA were against it. I don't recall asking their permission, so I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have a -- minutes of a meeting here where you didn't mention the KLA per se, but you were wondering why people in the field would be against a Planeja office or an office in the field. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had several discussions with the authorities about the Planeja. My sense was that Planeja was, inside -- indeed, inside the 5 kilometre border boundaries; but I still felt that it would be important to set up a field office there to enable us to monitor, if indeed there were infiltrations through the border, that would allow us to see firsthand these infiltrations to be able to report them to KVM headquarters. And if they were, you know, facilitated by the Albanian authorities, that would again put pressure on the Albanian authorities. On the other hand, it would also allow us to verify, to observe, the behaviour of the authorities and be able to report on their good behaviour or their bad behaviour as the case may be. So this would have been, to my sense, an important field office to set up. And that was, you know -- the entire time I was in Kosovo, that was the idea, to be able to have a good coverage of the area, to be able to observe properly, to be able to report, to verify in an impartial manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have here the minutes of a meeting you had with Commander Drini on the 26th of February. I am interested in something he says here. He says that "the 12-year-old boys conveyed the message."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document in front of me, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 873, I believe. In the English, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To make it easier for you, I'll read out the B/C/S translation: "If they shoot tomorrow, we will return fire, but we will not open fire first." Then there is a mention of Praga and Pirana. And then it says: "12-year-old boys conveyed the message."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where in the meeting report is that, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The 12th capital letter from the top. "Boys of 12 years passed ..." [In English] "If they" --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they fire tomorrow, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. So the last sentence: "Boys of 12 years passed message."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay now you've made the thing so big -- okay. There it is. Okay. Could you go back up please, a little bit. Yeah, I don't know what he's -- I have no recollection what he was referring to there, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that KLA members operated in civilian clothes without uniforms as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you said that your source in Albania on the number of refugees was the Albanian government concerning your report of the 18th of May. The Albanian government saw it as in their interest to have the number of refugees as large as possible to receive more aid, wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what I actually stated was that the government of Albania was at the source of the reporting, but also they were -- the UNHCR were on the ground, a number -- the ICRC, a number of NGOs also. And we had contact ourselves with all these agencies. And there was a systematic manner of reporting the number of refugees. As they crossed the border, they were counted, et cetera. And so I have a -- quite a bit of confidence in the figures that are in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you also said that you received great technical assistance from the staff that transferred from Kosovo to Albania, those of them who crossed over from Kosovo to Albania on the 24th of March and that they spoke good Albanian and could therefore take good quality statements. Am I right in saying that you are there referring to Albanian nationals or people of Albanian ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, the approach we took, of course, when we went into -- when we went into Albania at the end of March to look after the refugees, we brought with us some folks who were able to speak Albanian, but we also recruited local employees in Albania, per se, that we used as interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was the driver of Mr. Drewienkiewicz and Walker during their stay in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I sometimes may pronounce things incorrectly, but I think his name was Hajziri [phoen], and apparently he was a link between the Kosovo Verification Mission in Macedonia and the KLA, and that he forwarded all KLA information to the KVM. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The first report we saw which is P874, encompasses the period between the 2nd and the 15th of April, 1999, whereas your staff went in the field on the 5th of April, according to the report.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Therefore the information was retroactive; it was gathered before their stay in the field.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. And as I've mentioned before, the collation of this information was actually done by -- through our contact with the NGOs that were already deployed on the ground, those that had been there since the 24th of March and before. And the OSCE presence in Albania as well, direct contact. So the idea was to report on the two-week period, but you are right, some of that information had been gleaned and gathered from those that were on the ground before that we had -- that we cooperated with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you ever see a list of persons that were killed in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I conclude then that you don't know the age breakdown of the victims?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one last question for you: Do you know Mr. Richard Vabit or Wabit [phoen] who is also a Canadian and was in Pec? Have you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not. But I might have known him at the time; it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I'd still like to hear your comment regarding something. The organisation -- the type of organisation resembles the Italian mafia, that is to say, by families. The male family members stay close to their homes every day, digging trenches, making bunkers, and carrying out tactical training. Their food is prepared and brought to them by the female members of the family. In a family, there is one main person, a capo. The family members working abroad have their monthly payments due to be sent to the family. All that money can be channeled into purchasing weapons freely because food and medication is provided for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that my learned friend is reading from a document. I really -- he has not indicated what is the source of this passage he is reading, he has also put quite a lot of information to the witness, I'm not sure that there is a question here in the passage that he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He was interrupted before he reached the question, Ms. Kravetz, but the source of the document, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our exhibit -- rather document, it's not an exhibit, D003-1006. I would like to hear from the witness whether he is familiar with the contents of this document and whether he would agree with it. I believe the answer may be short. We don't have a translation, otherwise I would have put it up on the screen. The gentleman does not read that language, that's why I read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: General, you are asked whether you are familiar with this document and its contents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, that is the answer I expected to receive. General, thank you very much. It was a pleasure to speak to you. Your Honours, Defence concludes its cross-examination pursuant to your order. I have an objection to make though. It happened on several occasions that the Prosecutor brings witnesses whose testimony is limited in terms of time. This witness was at our disposal as of yesterday morning. Before him, we had a witness who was not limited in terms of time as opposed to this witness. We used most of yesterday with his testimony prior to reaching this witness to be put at our disposal by the Prosecutor. I do not believe that should be the practice we should follow in the future, and I would still like to thank the Chamber for considering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will discuss the matter you raise at some time when we are not pressed. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I please have Exhibit P837 back up on the screen, and I would like page 3 of the English and also page 3 of the B/C/S, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, you were asked several questions about this document that's going to appear on the screen, this is the Clark-Naumann Agreement. You were asked about the paragraph that precedes paragraph 8. And my questions relate to paragraph 8 specifically. We see that this paragraph says that: "In order to ensure verification of these provisions, VJ and MUP providers will provide ..." and if we read the second part of this paragraph, it says: "... will provide immediate notification to KDOM/OSCE of any deployments contrary to these provisions and will explain the circumstances regarding such deployments?" Now, you have told us that you were familiar at the time with this agreement. In your understanding, this expression "any deployments," would that have included deployment outside of barracks for the purpose of conducting training exercises?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So in your understanding -- and you were answering a question from my learned colleague with regard to what was the source of you saying that prior authorisation was required for conducting training exercises, you said that in your understanding you required prior coordination with the KVM and that was in one of the agreements that was shown earlier. Is this what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see the first part of this paragraph also refers to another requirement: "VJ commanders and MUP commanders will provide KDOM and OSCE with detailed weekly reports of manning, weapons, and activities of their forces." Was this a requirement that during your tenure in Kosovo was complied with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the second part that we were just discussing, the immediate notification of deployments contrary to the provisions of this agreement, was that something that was complied with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And in which circumstances was that complied with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were circumstances in which we understood that they would not be able to comply. For example, if they were provoked -- if the authorities were provoked by a particular incident, then we felt in the KVM that it was understandable that they would not have preplanned their deployments outside to react to a particular incident. So when that happened, we understood that, you know, it was part of their, you know, their reaction that they would do this, and then so we did not actually, you know, hold it against them from that point of view. But it happened quite often that they would take, for example, their tanks on the road and would really instill fear in the population, and we would go and protest, go and find out why they were doing this; and they would say it's driver training. Now, obviously if we had been warned ahead of time that this kind activity was going to be taking place, we could have warned the local population, we could have ensured that we were in different villages to reassure them that this was an agreed activity. So we never really got any of that prior notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now turn to the next page. And this is Roman numeral III. My learned colleague asked you a couple of questions in regard to this, and while you were being asked these questions - this is at transcript page of today 45, lines 18 and 19 - you said that the operative terms in the last part of this paragraph were the words "adequately and proportionately." Can you explain what you meant by that statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my view when I mean -- when I say adequately and proportionately, I guess I felt that definitely there were times when the Serb authorities would be provoked into taking certain actions, into reacting. For example, the incident, I believe, on the 8th of January, where a convoy of MUP vehicles was ambushed by the KLA, two policemen died on the scene, I believe, and one later. And the reaction by the Serb authorities was to bring a tank out of the Dulje position and to start firing into a village. And, you know, I just -- I had a hard time kind of calling that a proportionate or adequate response to an activity that, you know, wasn't really linked. And so this was kind of the type of incident that -- or the type of reaction that, to me, went against this adequately and proportionately operative words in this accord.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph refers to UN Security Council Resolution 1199 and you were asked some questions about that. And specifically, my learned colleague asked you about a phrase that refers to not carrying out any repressive actions against a peaceful population - and he asked you this is at transcript page 38, lines 7 and 8 - if the populations were not peaceful, was there no ban on any measures taken against them, and you said that's the way you read it as well. Now, based on the answer you just provided us, to your understanding of this Roman numeral III, would there have been restrictions on the way Serb authorities could react when provoked or when perceived to be provoked?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would think that the restriction is exactly those three words "adequately and proportionately." So meaning that the restriction would be that the reaction would be in proportionality to the level of the attack or the provocation, i.e., if you are fired by a small arms, you know, a couple of small arms shots from a particular village, you don't deploy an entire company to go do it, to go and react to that. On the other hand, if you're -- if you're attacked from a village by 20 or 30, I think as the counsel spoke earlier, then obviously the reaction by a company might be appropriate and adequate. So this to me were the kinds of -- the kinds of restrictions that formed part of this accord.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now moving on to a different topic. My learned colleague asked you today when you were speaking about military structures and MUP structures and your familiarity with both of them, he asked you why you knew military structures in your area better than you did MUP, and you said that you variously associated with military structures such as brigade more than you -- and not so easily with paramilitary like the MUP. This is at page 30, line 21. What did you mean when you were referring to the MUP as a paramilitary structure?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm referring to here is that I see, I certainly assessed in my own mind the MUP as being not just a police force, but also a kind of a police force with more, if you wish, much like a Gendarmerie in France where they're able to do almost infantry type tactics, they're able to -- they have armoured vehicles, they are equipped with some heavier weapons than just a straight pistols that you would find in, say, a strictly police type force. So to me they were, if you wish, between the police and the military, they were kind of an in-between organisation, so that's why I call them paramilitary. In my country, we don't have such forces. Our police are, you know, don't usually travel in armoured vehicles. They don't do infantry tactics. In fact, when they try to do infantry tactics, they don't do so well. And there have been incidents of deaths and so on of police who tried to do this kind of thing. So we have a more, if you wish, a clearer definition between police forces, military forces, and so to my mind my assessment is the MUP was somewhere in middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And just one final issue I wanted to get to before this session ends today. I would like to refer you to attachment 13A of your statement, and this is Exhibit P870. Now, today you were asked -- well, I'll first let you get to that document.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- this is kind of a -- an assessment, a report that I put together after the incidents of Racak and Stimlje on the -- I believe, the evening of the 16th of January. That's a report I wrote myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, today at page 60, you were asked by my learned colleague about whether you had been shown any reports prepared by verifiers in relation to the Racak incident, and you said that you didn't recall seeing any in this courtroom but you referred to preparing your own reports and having spoken to verifiers for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this the report that you were speaking about when you were providing that answer to my learned colleague? Or were you speaking about another document?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is certainly, this is certainly one of the -- one of the documents I was referring to, and I don't recall exactly, but there must have been a daily sitrep also prepared by my regional centre and sent up to the KVM, but I don't recall it immediately at this point, so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see the second bullet point below the date 16th January, this is like in the middle of the page. It says: "Head RC 1 Prizren arrived on the scene at 9 a.m. and was briefed by head CC 3." I take it the reference to head RC 1 Prizren, that would be a reference to yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you were speaking and responding to my learn colleague and said that you had been in close contact and had discussions with the verifiers, would this paragraph be -- this paragraph be an example of the type of information you received from the verifiers on the ground that you later included in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we look at bullet point 3 from the bottom, it says: "Head RC 1 proceeds further into the village..." And you referred to bodies you observed and the ages of -- and the sex of the bodies that you observed. Would this report have also contained your personal observations on-site in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are you down in the third bullet before the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, where it says: "Head RC 1 proceeds further into the village..."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly -- that was me, head RC 1, and I did proceed into the village, and I observed the bodies of four more individuals as stated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are nearing the end of this session so those are my questions for the witness; I'll stop at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, you'll be pleased to know, A, that is the end of the questions; B, we finished within time; C, you are clear to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would like to thank you for your attendance once again and for the assistance that you've been able to give us in this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dealing very quickly with the matter you raised, Mr. Djurdjic, there may be a problem, and we have mentioned it where there is a witness who is under a time limitation, ensuring that that is known as the time for that witness to give evidence approaches or as the witness is giving evidence so that we can adjust time proceedings to accommodate that. Equally though, the situation in this case was due partly to the time taken with the two witnesses before that, which was longer than might reasonably be thought necessary, so that this witness was reached later in the week than could have been reasonably anticipated. Even so, we were, I believe, careful to make it known to both counsel that there was a time limitation, and we went to some lengths to ensure that you had a reasonable time for your questions, which is the course we would take. As I have mentioned to counsel before, the Chamber is not inclined to impose strict time-limits. If it did so, this particular sort of problem might rarely, if ever, arise. But if it did so, counsel would find themselves much more limited than they are now with virtually every witness. We prefer to allow it to the judgement and responsibility of counsel to adjust time to what is really necessary. In view of those matters, I don't think there was anything out of proper management in the timing of this witness. It seems to the Chamber that there was a reasonable opportunity given to Defence, a time probably much longer than might have been available before some other Trial Chambers. And we continue, though, to urge the Prosecution to make known if a witness has a particular time limitation in time for any adjustment that might be necessary to be made. We adjourn now. We continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.
